in_context.text: Paul has just said that elders who lead well, especially those who preach and teach, deserve "double honour" (5:17). This verse gives the reason: two sayings showing that those who work should be supported by their work. The next verses turn to how to handle accusations against elders (5:19-20).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer. He quotes "the scripture" for the first saying, and the second saying matches words of Jesus.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: The church's elders who rule well and labour in the word and doctrine, and the believers who are to support them.

what.text: Paul quotes the Law of Moses: an ox treading out grain must not be muzzled, so it can eat as it works. He adds that a worker deserves his wages. Together they show that church leaders who work hard at teaching should be supported, as Paul argues the same way in 1 Corinthians 9.

events.text: The instruction applies to the ongoing life of the church at Ephesus while Timothy led it, after Paul had gone on to Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, by Paul, between his Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and see it as written in Paul's name by a follower; others defend Paul's authorship and the earlier date.

where.text: The letter was sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. The place of writing is not stated, though Paul may have written from Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul wants Timothy to treat faithful elders fairly, including giving them material support, as part of ordering the church as God's household.

big_picture.text: Chapter 5 is about caring for groups in the church: widows, elders, and others. Just as families should provide for their own (5:8), the church should provide for those who labour among them in teaching.

for_readers.text: Scripture's concern for fair pay runs deep: even working animals were to eat, and hired workers were to be paid promptly. Paul applies that fairness to those who teach God's word.

why_it_matters.text: The Greek word here properly means wages or hire. So "reward" in the KJV means pay earned for work, not a prize or a heavenly reward.
The word first meant a field worker, fitting the farming picture of the ox. It is also used elsewhere of Christian teachers, which ties the image to elders who labour in teaching.
To muzzle is to block the mouth so the animal cannot eat. The point is that the worker should be allowed to benefit from the very work being done.
The singular word often points to a particular written passage of the sacred writings. Paul grounds his instruction in written Scripture, not just his own opinion.

takeaway.text: This verse is not a general saying about rewards. It backs up Paul's call to honour and support elders who lead and teach well, using God's own rule that workers, even oxen, should share in the fruit of their labour.
